newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chocolate importers struggle with weak mark.
newsitem.headline: German chocolate importers struggle with weak mark.

text.p: German confectionery importers said the mark's weakness was making business difficult in early 1997 following struggles in 1996, when higher buying-in prices could not be passed on to consumers.
Uwe Lebens of the Confectionery Wholesale and Foreign Trade Federation (BSGA) said importers were also faced with competitive domestic prices and high logistics costs.
He was speaking at a news conference ahead of the ISM confectionery trade fair, which runs January 26-30 and will feature 330 domestic and 1,032 foreign sweets manufacturers.
Chocolate firms account for 600 of the total of 1,362.
Lebens' remarks were not borne out by BSGA import figures, which were only available for the first half of 1996 and therefore did not fully reflect the currency problems.

Chocolate and sweets figures in January-June 1996, not counting ice cream, increased by 11 percent both in tonnage (193,750 tonnes) and in value (1.07 billion marks) versus the comparable 1995 period.
Imports accounted for 17.5 percent of total domestic confectionery sales and the share of imports from other EU countries was 88 percent.

Lebens said the the higher import figures did not point to higher demand as exports were also high and some production capacity had been shifted around by companies operating throughout the European Union.

Lebens also said a trend in recent years towards the widening of chocolate sales outlets away from supermarkets to petrol stations and kiosks had slowed in 1996. Its impact on total demand was now neutral.
